text: Lesson 25 ended with a five-step sketch for Contractor Offboarding. Now you'll actually build it in Flow Designer — and every mechanism it needs, from branching to subflows to approvals, you've already learned in an earlier chapter. This lesson is about sequencing those pieces correctly, not learning anything brand new.

Open a flow scoped to the contractor table, with the scheduled trigger from Lesson 25 already set: daily, querying for an end date of today and an active status. The first action is an If/Else on contractor type. IT contractors typically have accounts in more systems — a VPN profile, elevated roles, maybe a service account — while non-IT contractors usually just need their base network account disabled. The branch exists because the two paths genuinely need different handling, not for its own sake.

Both branches then call the same Revoke Access subflow. It takes the contractor's user record as its Input and hands back a revocation status as its Output. The calling flow doesn't need to know how the subflow revokes access internally — only that it did, and what the result was. After the subflow returns, an Approval action routes to the contractor's manager to confirm equipment was returned, and a Create Record action creates an IT task summarizing what happened and what still needs a human to finish.

Building Revoke Access as its own subflow matters beyond tidiness. That same subflow could later be called from a completely different flow — a security-incident response, for instance — without rebuilding any of this logic. That reusability is exactly the argument for a subflow over inline logic.

That's the whole flow built: a scheduled trigger, a branch, a reusable subflow, an approval, and a task — five mechanisms from earlier chapters, sequenced into one real process instead of five separate labs. Next, Lesson 27 verifies it actually works and writes it up as real documentation.
